reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Ptosis is abnormal drooping of the upper eyelid; severity is gauged by the margin-reflex distance and the effect on the visual axis
Assessing levator function is central to classification and surgical planning
Aponeurotic (involutional) ptosis is the commonest, showing good levator function, a high skin crease, and often thinning of the eyelid
A ptosis with a small pupil and ipsilateral anhidrosis suggests Horner syndrome; a ptosis with a dilated pupil and an eye deviated down and out suggests a third nerve palsy
Variable, fatigable ptosis worsening through the day points to myasthenia gravis and warrants systemic evaluation
Congenital ptosis usually reflects levator dystrophy with poor function and risks amblyopia if the visual axis is occluded in a child
The rare Marcus Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon links lid elevation to jaw movement
reference.pathophysiology: Ptosis results from impaired elevation of the upper lid, which is normally raised by the levator palpebrae superioris (oculomotor nerve) and Muller muscle (sympathetic). Aponeurotic ptosis is caused by dehiscence or stretching of the levator aponeurosis with age. Neurogenic ptosis follows interruption of the nerve supply, as in third nerve palsy or sympathetic denervation (Horner syndrome). Myogenic ptosis reflects muscle disease such as myasthenia gravis, chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, or myotonic dystrophy. Mechanical ptosis arises from lid mass or scarring, and congenital ptosis from maldevelopment of the levator muscle.
additionalDifferentials: Myasthenia gravis and other myogenic causes
Mechanical ptosis from lid mass or oedema
Pseudoptosis from dermatochalasis, brow ptosis, or contralateral lid retraction
additionalInvestigations: Measurement of margin-reflex distance, palpebral aperture, levator function, and skin crease position
Pupil examination to identify Horner syndrome or third nerve palsy
Assessment for fatigability and ice-pack or targeted testing when myasthenia is suspected
Neuroimaging when a compressive or neurogenic cause is suspected
Systemic and antibody testing for suspected myasthenia gravis
redFlags: Painful ptosis with a dilated pupil and ophthalmoplegia suggesting a compressive third nerve palsy (possible aneurysm) requiring urgent imaging
Ptosis with anisocoria and anhidrosis (Horner syndrome), which may indicate serious underlying pathology such as an apical lung lesion or carotid dissection
Fatigable or variable ptosis with diplopia or bulbar symptoms suggesting myasthenia gravis
Ptosis occluding the visual axis in a child, threatening amblyopia
reference.prognosis: Aponeurotic and congenital ptosis generally respond well to surgery; the outlook for neurogenic and myogenic ptosis depends on the underlying cause, and childhood ptosis carries a risk of amblyopia if not managed promptly.
pitfalls: Treating ptosis as purely cosmetic and missing a serious neurological cause such as third nerve palsy or Horner syndrome
Failing to test for fatigability and overlooking myasthenia gravis
Not recognising amblyopia risk in congenital ptosis
Mistaking pseudoptosis from brow droop or dermatochalasis for true ptosis
management: Direct treatment at the underlying mechanism, which differs for aponeurotic, neurogenic, myogenic and mechanical ptosis
Levator advancement or resection surgery for aponeurotic and congenital ptosis with adequate levator function, and a frontalis sling when levator function is poor
Urgently evaluate a painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil to exclude a compressive aneurysm, and investigate Horner syndrome for its cause
Treat myasthenia gravis medically with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and immunosuppression before considering lid surgery, since the ptosis fluctuates
In children, correct promptly when the visual axis is occluded to prevent amblyopia, with orthoptic follow-up
Remove or treat mechanical causes such as lid masses or scarring
Ophthalmology and oculoplastic referral, with neurology input for neurogenic and myogenic causes
